name: Identify Purpose
explanation: This criterion extends the idea of "identify purpose" beyond form fields, covered by SC 1.3.5, to the broader set of icons, regions, and components that make up a page. When an icon or region has a well-known, standardized purpose, like a search icon or a "main navigation" region, that purpose should be identifiable in code, not just conveyed by its visual appearance. In practice this means using semantic HTML and ARIA to expose what things are: landmark roles for regions, and an accessible name for icon-only controls. This lets assistive technology and user-customization tools recognize and adapt these elements automatically. A symbol-set browser extension that swaps in pictograms for people with cognitive or language disabilities is one example — it can only do that when the underlying purpose is exposed in code.
whoItAffects: This affects people with cognitive, language, or learning disabilities who rely on symbol-support browser extensions that replace text and icons with familiar pictograms. Those tools can only substitute the right symbol when the underlying purpose is exposed in code, not just implied by a generic-looking icon. It affects screen reader users navigating by landmark when a page uses only visual layout instead of semantic regions, since there is nothing to jump to. It also affects screen reader and switch-access users encountering icon-only buttons, like a trash-can or gear icon, with no accessible name — they hear only "button" with no indication of what pressing it does. People with low vision using screen magnification benefit too, since landmark navigation lets them jump directly to a page region without visually scanning the full layout.

howToTest: Use the keyboard or a screen reader's landmark list to check that major page regions — navigation, search, main content, footer — show up as named landmarks rather than being absent. Then tab to every icon-only control on the page and listen to what your screen reader announces, or check the browser's accessibility inspector for an accessible name. It fails if it announces only "button" with no indication of purpose, even if the icon looks self-explanatory to a sighted user.

check.question: A page has a `<div>` styled to look like a navigation bar containing links, and a trash-can icon `<button>` with no text or `aria-label`. Which best explains why this fails SC 1.3.6 (Level AAA)?
choices: It doesn't fail, because the icon and the div's visual styling make their purpose obvious to any user
It fails because neither the region's purpose (navigation) nor the icon button's purpose (delete) is exposed in a way assistive technology or symbol-substitution tools can read
It fails only because the div lacks a landmark role; the icon button is fine since icons are self-explanatory
It fails only because the icon button lacks a label; unmarked divs are always acceptable for layout
